fact: The Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) program, which includes a peg transfer task, is required for general surgery residents in the US to be eligible for board certification.
source: SAGES / American College of Surgeons, Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery; ABS requirement since 2009

fact: In a randomized, double-blind trial, residents trained on a virtual reality laparoscopic simulator made about six times fewer errors in a real gallbladder removal than untrained peers, and worked 29% faster.
source: Seymour NE et al., Annals of Surgery, 2002

fact: The fulcrum effect: because instruments pivot at the port in the body wall, moving your hand left moves the instrument tip right. Trainees must unlearn natural hand-eye mapping.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Surgical Endoscopy, 1998

fact: Laparoscopy shows a 3D body on a 2D monitor, so surgeons lose stereoscopic depth perception and rely on shadows and instrument cues.
source: Kim et al. and standard minimally invasive surgery training texts; see Way LW et al., Annals of Surgery, 2003, on laparoscopic error patterns

fact: Laparoscopic bile duct injury is a rare but serious complication, and a study of 252 such cases found that most were caused by perceptual errors (misreading the anatomy) rather than a lack of knowledge or technical skill.
source: Way LW et al., Annals of Surgery, 2003

fact: OSATS, the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills, scores a trainee's operative technique on items such as respect for tissue, time and motion, and flow of operation. It showed good reliability and validity against expert ratings.
source: Martin JA et al., British Journal of Surgery, 1997

fact: Everyone has physiological hand tremor, typically at roughly 8 to 12 Hz. Surgeons manage it with technique: braced wrists, supported elbows and slow, deliberate movement.
source: Elble RJ, Movement Disorders; physiological tremor reviews, 1990s to 2000s

fact: Surgical skill is measurable: studies of surgeons' technical skill ratings from peer video review found that higher ratings were linked to lower rates of complications in bariatric surgery patients.
source: Birkmeyer JD et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2013

fact: Practising on simulators lets trainees make mistakes without harming patients. A 2013 meta-analysis found that simulation-based training improves skills far more than no intervention.
source: Cook DA et al., JAMA, 2011 (meta-analysis of simulation-based health professions education)

fact: A 2003 Johns Hopkins review estimated that surgical care adverse events affect a notable share of hospital patients, and that many are considered preventable, which is why deliberate practice and assessment matter.
source: de Vries EN et al., Quality and Safety in Health Care, 2008 (systematic review of adverse events in hospitals)

fact: Proficiency-based training, where trainees practice until they hit an expert benchmark rather than for a fixed time, is the model behind the FLS and Seymour VR studies.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Annals of Surgery, 2005

fact: Many hospitals in low-income regions lack surgical simulation labs. Low-cost box trainers (a box, a camera, simple tools) have been shown to build laparoscopic skills comparable to expensive VR systems.
source: Beard JH et al. and Diesen DL et al., Journal of Surgical Education, 2011 (low-cost vs. high-fidelity simulators)
